title: Ants, burdens and the image of God
source_text: Εἰπὼν δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος περὶ τῶν μελισσῶν, ἵνα τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ ἐξευτελίσῃ ἡμῶν οὐ Χριστιανῶν μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὰς πολιτείας καὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἡγεμονίας καὶ τοὺς ὑπὲρ τῶν πατρίδων πολέμους, ἑξῆς ἐπιφέρει διεξιὼν μυρμήκων ἐγκώμιον· ὅπως τῷ περὶ ἐκείνων ἐγκωμίῳ τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων περὶ τὴν τροφὴν οἰκονομικὸν καταβάλῃ τῷ λόγῳ (τῷ) πρὸς τοὺς μύρμηκας καὶ τὸ τῶν χειμαδίων προνοητικὸν καταῤῥίψῃ ὡς οὐδὲν πλέον ἔχον τῆς ἀλόγου τῶν μυρμήκων ἐν οἷς ἐκεῖνος νομίζει προνοίας. τίνα δ᾿ οὐκ ἂν τῶν ἁπλουστέρων ἀνθρώπων καὶ οὐκ ἐπισταμένων ἐνορᾶν τῇ φύσει πάντων πραγμάτων ἀποτρέψαι τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ ὁ Κέλσος ἀπὸ τοῦ (τοῖς) βαρουμένοις ὑπὸ φορτίων βοηθεῖν καὶ κοινωνεῖν ἐκείνοις τῶν καμάτων, λέγων περὶ μυρμήκων ὡς ἂν ἀλλήλοις τῶν φορτίων, ἐπειδάν τινα κάμνοντα ἴδωσιν, ἐπιλαμβάνωνται; ἐρεῖ γὰρ ὁ δεόμενος τῆς διὰ λόγου παιδεύσεως καὶ μηδαμῶς ἐπαΐων αὐτῆς· ἐπεὶ τοίνυν μηδὲν διαφέρομεν μυρμήκων, καὶ ὅτε τοῖς κάμνουσι διὰ τὸ φέρειν βαρύτατα φορτία βοηθοῦμεν, τί μάτην τὸ τοιοῦτον ποιοῦμεν; καὶ οἱ μὲν μύρμηκες, ἅτε ἄλογα ζῷα τυγχάνοντες, οὐκ ἂν ἐπαρθεῖεν πρὸς τὸ μέγα φρονῆσαι διὰ τὸ παραβάλλεσθαι ἀνθρώποις τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν· οἱ δ᾿ ἄνθρωποι διὰ τὸν λόγον ἀκοῦσαι δυνηθέντες, τίνα τρόπον εὐτε λίζεται αὐτῶν τὸ κοινωνικὸν. βλαβεῖεν ἂν τὸ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ, οὐκ ἰδόντι ὅτι χριστιανισμοῦ ἀποτρέψαι θέλων τοὺς ἐντυγχάνοντας αὐτοῦ τῇ γραφῇ ἀποτρέπει καὶ τῶν οὐ Χριστιανῶν τὸ πρὸς τοὺς φέροντας τὰ βαρύτατα τῶν φορτίων συμπαθές. ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν, εἴπερ ην κἂν φιλόσοφος αἰσθανόμενος τοῦ κοινωνικοῦ, πρὸς τῷ (μὴ) συναναιρεῖν τῷ χριστιανισμῷ τὰ χρήσιμα τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις καὶ συνεργεῖν, εἰ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν, τοῖς κοινοῖς ἐν χριστιανισμῷ πρὸς τοὺς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους καλοῖς. εἰ δὲ καὶ τῶν ἀποτιθεμένων καρπῶν τὰς ἐκφύσεις ἀπεκτιθέασιν οἱ μύρμηκες, ἵνα μὴ σπαργῷεν. μένοιεν δὲ δι᾿ ἔτους αὐτοῖς εἰς τροφὴν, οὐ λογισμὸν εἶναι ἐν μύρμηξι τούτων αἴτιον ὑπονοητέον ἀλλὰ τὴν παμμήτορα φύσιν, καὶ τὰ ἄλογα κοσμήσασαν, ὡς μηδὲ τοὐλάχιστον καταλιπεῖν, μηδαμῶς φέρον ἴχνος τοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως λόγου. εἰ μὴ ἄρα διὰ τούτων λεληθότως βούλεται ὁ Κέλσος (καὶ γὰρ ἐν πολλοῖς Πλατωνίζειν θέλει) ὁμοειδῆ εἶναι πᾶσαν ψυχὴν, καὶ μηδὲν διαφέρειν τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τῆς τῶν μυρμήκων καὶ τῶν μελισσῶν· ὅπερ κατάγοντός ἐστι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἁψίδων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ οὐκ ἐπὶ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον σῶμα μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ λοιπά. τούτοις δ᾿ οὐ πείσονται Χριστιανοὶ. προκατειληφότες τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα“ γεγονέναι θεοῦ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ψυχὴν καὶ ὁρῶντες ὅτι ἀμήχανόν ἐστι τὴν „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα“ θεοῦ δεδημιουργημένην φύσιν πάντῃ ἀπαλεῖψαι τοὺς χαρακτῆρας αὐτῆς καὶ ἄλλους ἀναλαβεῖν οὐκ οἶδα κατ᾿ εἰκόνας τίνων γεγενημένους ἐν τοῖς ἀλόγοις.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus, having spoken about the bees, in order that he may cheapen (ἐξευτελίζω), as far as in him, the cities and the constitutions and the offices and the leaderships and the wars on behalf of the fatherlands (πατρίς) of us, not of Christians only but of all men, next adds (ἐπιφέρω), going through (διέξειμι) a eulogy (ἐγκώμιον) of ants; so that by the eulogy about them he may throw down (καταβάλλω) the managing (οἰκονομικόν) of men about food (τροφή) by the comparison (λόγος) with ants, and cast down (καταρρίπτω) the provident (προνοητικόν) [care] of winter quarters (χειμάδιον) as having nothing more than the irrational providence of ants in what he supposes (νομίζω). Whom of the simpler (ἁπλούστερος) men, and not knowing (ἐπίσταμαι) how to look into (ἐνοράω) the nature of all things (πράγματα), would Celsus not turn away (ἀποτρέπω), as far as in him, from helping (βοηθέω) those weighed down (βαρέω) by burdens (φορτίον) and sharing (κοινωνέω) with them their toils (κάματος), saying about ants that they take hold of (ἐπιλαμβάνομαι) one another's burdens, whenever they see someone wearying (κάμνω)? For the one needing (δέομαι) the education (παίδευσις) through reason and in no way perceiving (ἐπαΐω) it will say: 'since then we differ in nothing from ants, even when we help those wearied through carrying heaviest burdens, why do we do such a thing in vain (μάτην)?' And the ants, being irrational animals, would not be lifted up (ἐπαίρω) toward thinking great (μέγα φρονέω) because their works are compared (παραβάλλω) with men; but men, able through reason to hear in what way their sociability (τὸ κοινωνικόν) is cheapened (εὐτελίζω), would be harmed (βλάπτω), as far as depends on Celsus and his words, who did not see that, wishing to turn away from Christianity (χριστιανισμός) those who read (ἐντυγχάνω) his writing (γραφή), he turns away also the sympathy (τὸ συμπαθές) of non-Christians toward those carrying the heaviest of burdens. It was needful (ἐχρῆν) for him, if he were even a philosopher perceiving the social (τὸ κοινωνικόν), besides not destroying together (συναναιρέω) with Christianity the useful things among men, also to work together (συνεργέω), if it were possible, with the common goods (κοινὰ καλά) in Christianity toward the other men. And if also the ants put out/remove (ἀπεκτίθημι) the outgrowths (ἔκφυσις) of the stored (ἀποτίθημι) fruits (καρπός), that they may not swell (σπαργάω), but remain (μένω) through the year for them for food, not reasoning (λογισμός) in ants is to be suspected (ὑπονοητέον) as cause (αἴτιον) of these, but the all-mother (παμμήτωρ) nature, having ordered (κοσμέω) even the irrational, so as to leave behind not even the least (τοὐλάχιστον) in no way bearing a trace (ἴχνος) of the reason from nature. Unless then (εἰ μὴ ἄρα) through these Celsus covertly (λεληθότως) wishes (for in many things he wishes to Platonize, Πλατωνίζω) every soul (ψυχή) to be of the same form (ὁμοειδής), and the man's to differ in nothing from that of ants and bees; which is of one bringing down (κατάγω) the soul from the vaults (ἁψίς) of heaven not onto the human body only but also onto the rest. By these Christians will not be persuaded (πείθομαι), having grasped beforehand (προκαταλαμβάνω) that the human soul has come to be 'according to the image' (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα) of God, and seeing that it is impossible (ἀμήχανον) for the nature fashioned (δημιουργέω) 'according to the image' of God altogether (πάντῃ) to wipe out (ἀπαλείφω) its features/stamps (χαρακτήρ) and take up (ἀναλαμβάνω) others, come to be according to images of I know not whom (οὐκ οἶδα τίνων), in the irrational.
pass_b_english: Having spoken of the bees, in order to belittle, as far as he can, the cities, constitutions, offices and governments, and the wars for the fatherland, not of us Christians only but of all men, Celsus next goes on to set out a eulogy of ants. His aim is that by praising them he may overthrow, through his comparison with ants, men’s careful management of their food, and cast down their forethought in providing for winter as having nothing more in it than the irrational foresight he supposes ants to have.

Which of the simpler sort of people, who do not know how to look into the nature of all things, would Celsus not turn aside, as far as he can, from helping those weighed down by burdens and sharing their toils, when he says of ants that “whenever they see one of them tiring, they take up one another’s loads”? For a man who needs the training that comes through reason, and has no understanding of it, will say: “Since, then, we differ in nothing from ants even when we help those who are worn out from carrying very heavy loads, why should we do such a thing to no purpose?”

Ants, being irrational animals, would not be lifted up to think highly of themselves because their works are compared with those of men. But men, who through reason are able to hear how their fellow-feeling is being belittled, would be harmed, as far as it rests with Celsus and his words. He did not see that, in wishing to turn the readers of his book away from Christianity, he also discourages the compassion that even those who are not Christians feel toward people carrying the heaviest of loads. If he had been a philosopher with even some sense of human fellowship, he ought not only to have refrained from destroying, along with Christianity, what is useful among men, but also, if it were possible, to have lent his support to the good things that Christianity holds in common with other men.

And if ants also remove the sprouting parts of the grain they store up, so that it does not swell but lasts them through the year as food, we must not suppose that reasoning in the ants is the cause of this, but nature, the mother of all, which has ordered even irrational creatures, so as to leave not even the smallest thing without some trace of the reason that comes from nature.

Unless, perhaps, Celsus covertly means by this (for in many things he wants to follow Plato) that every soul is of the same kind, and that the soul of a man differs in nothing from that of ants and bees. This is the view of one who brings the soul down from the vault of heaven not into the human body alone, but into the other bodies as well. Christians will not be persuaded by this. They have already learned that the human soul was made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27), and they see that it is impossible for a nature fashioned “in the image” of God to wipe out its features entirely and take on others, made after the images of who knows what among the irrational creatures.

Celsus's claim about ants helping one another is reported in indirect speech (ὡς ... ἐπιλαμβάνωνται) and is put in quotation marks as his reported words. The objector's words ('Since, then, we differ...') are Origen's imagined speaker, not Celsus; quoted as direct speech as the Greek frames it (ἐρεῖ γάρ). The source prints εἴπερ ην, read ἦν; ⟨τοῖς⟩, ⟨τῷ⟩ and ⟨μὴ⟩ are Koetschau's supplements and are followed (without ⟨μὴ⟩ the sentence would say the opposite, 'besides destroying'). ἀπεκτιθέασιν is an odd form ('put out, remove'); rendered 'remove' by sense, since Celsus evidently said ants cut off the sprouts of stored grain. σπαργῷεν ('swell') rendered literally. The double negative ὡς μηδὲ τοὐλάχιστον καταλιπεῖν μηδαμῶς φέρον ἴχνος is taken as 'leave not even the smallest thing without a trace of reason'. 'The vault of heaven' (ἁψῖδες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) echoes Plato, Phaedrus 247b (ὑπουράνιος ἁψίς), and the descent of souls into animal bodies recalls Phaedrus 249b; allusions, not quotations, so not cited inline. 'In the image' of God: Genesis 1:27 (LXX κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ; compare 1:26). Helping the burdened may recall Galatians 6:2 ('Bear one another's burdens'), but Origen uses no wording of that verse; possible allusion only, not cited inline.
